title: Unseasonal Rain Is Extending India's Dengue, Malaria and Flood-Disease Season
excerpt: Rainfall above roughly 100 mm a month lifts dengue risk toward 2.3 times baseline, mosquitoes are colonising hill districts, and leptospirosis follows every flood.
body:
• Unseasonal and shifting rainfall is extending India's vector and waterborne disease season, pushing dengue, malaria and Japanese encephalitis into high-altitude and semi-arid districts that rarely saw them.
  • A South Asia review found dengue risk rises above about 100 mm of monthly rain and peaks near 200 mm, at roughly 2.3 times the reference risk; India's pooled rainfall-linked risk estimate was 1.68.
  • Leptospirosis is the flood disease to watch: more than 85% of annual cases occur during and just after the monsoon, and Kerala recorded 1,318 cases with 53 deaths after the 2018 floods.
  • Household action: clear standing water weekly, boil or treat drinking water after flooding, and seek care early for fever after wading through floodwater.

India's disease calendar no longer follows the monsoon calendar. A multi-institutional risk review finds that volatile rainfall, intense local cloudbursts followed by humid dry spells, has let mosquitoes colonise sub-Himalayan and semi-arid western districts that were previously too cold or too dry for them, according to reporting summarised by SphereNexus.

The Rainfall Threshold

The dose matters, and it is measurable. A major South Asia review covered by Scienmag found dengue risk stays broadly flat below about 100 mm of monthly rainfall, then climbs, peaking near 200 mm at about 2.3 times the reference risk before plateauing. India's pooled estimate was 1.68, between Bangladesh at 2.13 and Sri Lanka at 1.42. Malaria showed a double peak, near 125 mm and 350 mm, consistent with moderate rain creating breeding pools and heavier rain first flushing habitats, then creating new ones.

Beyond Mosquitoes: the Flood Diseases

Water itself carries the second wave. Leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected animals, mainly rats, shows a strong seasonal pattern, with more than 85% of annual cases during and immediately after the monsoon. Flooding drives rats out of sewers and burrows into homes and drains, and the bacteria can survive in contaminated water or soil for weeks to months, Ashoka University's Gautam Menon and other experts told SphereNexus.

The historical marker is Kerala after the 2018 flood: 1,318 leptospirosis cases and 53 deaths, on Integrated Disease Surveillance Project data. In 2024, Pune reported a surge in Zika infections following heavy monsoon rain and flooding.

Why the Map Is Moving

Warmer conditions let mosquitoes survive and breed for longer, and warming shortens the time a pathogen needs inside the mosquito before it can infect a person. In the Himalayan foothills, malaria-carrying Anopheles mosquitoes now persist at elevations once considered too cold. Populations in those districts have little historical exposure, and therefore little immunity.

Drought is not safety either. Prolonged water shortages push households to store water in open containers, which creates exactly the breeding sites Aedes mosquitoes use.

What Households Should Do

The precautions are specific. Empty and scrub water-storage containers weekly. After any flooding, treat drinking water before use and avoid wading in floodwater with open cuts. Treat fever that follows floodwater exposure as urgent, and tell the doctor about the exposure, because leptospirosis is treatable early and dangerous late. The risk window now runs weeks beyond the last heavy rain, not just during it.
